Q1.answer: (a) Final rule: DHS/ICE, 'Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media,' FR document 2026-14439, 91 FR 44976–45131 (156 pages). (b) Published July 17, 2026; effective September 15, 2026 (DATES, 91 FR 44976). (c) Docket: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001; RIN 1653-AA95 (significant regulatory action). (d) It finalized the NPRM published as document 2025-16554, 90 FR 42070 (Aug. 28, 2025), same docket and RIN (preamble n.24, 91 FR 44978). (e) As of November 14, 2026 the effective date stands at September 15, 2026, and the rule's own text hard-codes that date (8 CFR 214.1(a)(4), (m)(1)). The DATES section notes the rule was classified as a major rule subject to congressional review and that 'at the conclusion of the congressional review, if the effective date has been changed, DHS will publish a document in the Federal Register to establish the actual effective date or to terminate the rule' (91 FR 44976). Searches of the docket (ICEB-2025-0001) and RIN 1653-AA95 from July 17 through November 14, 2026 return no correction, notice, or other document changing the effective date, and no presidential or congressional-review document naming the rule; so it could in principle still change (CRA disapproval or a DHS publication), but nothing in the Federal Register has changed it.
Q1.basis: 2026-14439 (91 FR 44976), DATES section and abstract; proposed rule 2025-16554 (90 FR 42070); FR docket/RIN searches, July 17–November 14, 2026.
Q1.uncertainty: The FR cannot show what Congress may do under the CRA or any non-FR litigation; the documents show only that no effective-date change has been published as of November 14, 2026.

Q2.answer: (a) Priya is covered by the D/S transition rule, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1): an F-1 admitted for D/S who is properly maintaining status on September 15, 2026 is authorized to remain until the later of EAD expiration (she has none) or the program end date on her I-20 (May 15, 2027), not to exceed 4 years from September 15, 2026, plus the 60-day F departure period. Arithmetic: program end May 15, 2027; +60 days (May 16–31 = 16 days, June = 30, July 1–14 = 14) = July 14, 2027. She may remain without filing anything through July 14, 2027. (b) The maximum dates are stated in 214.1(m)(1): F nonimmigrants — 4 years from September 15, 2026 is September 15, 2030, plus 60 days = November 14, 2030 (the rule states this date expressly); J nonimmigrants — September 15, 2030 plus 30 days = October 15, 2030. (c) Yes. Transfer timing: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G) requires that she begin classes at the transfer school within 5 months of transferring out or of the program completion date on her current I-20 (May 15, 2027), whichever is earlier. May 15, 2027 + 5 months = October 14, 2027; August 24, 2027 is about 3 months 10 days later, so the timing rule is satisfied. As a bachelor's-level student past her first academic year (she began in August 2023), the first-year bar in (f)(5)(ii)(A) does not apply. (d) Yes. Because her authorized stay ends (July 14, 2027) before the new program and its end date exceed her admission, she must file an extension of stay (Form I-539) with USCIS: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (transition students starting a new program 'must apply for an extension of stay with USCIS in accordance with paragraph (c)(2)'), 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) (form, fees, initial evidence, biometrics), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D) (change of educational objectives requires an EOS 'with the required fee' where one is sought), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv) (EOS for the new program), and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)–(B) (contents and receipt-by deadline — on or before expiration of her authorized stay, including the departure period, i.e., by July 14, 2027). (e) She files only Form I-765: because she is recommended for post-completion OPT and files before March 18, 2027, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) excuses her from filing an I-539 for the OPT period. If the OPT is approved as requested (EAD June 14, 2027–June 13, 2028), she may remain until the EAD expiration plus 60 days: June 13, 2028 + 60 days = August 12, 2028 (214.1(m)(1)(i)).
Q2.uncertainty: (c) The rule does not say expressly whether a transfer release date may fall after the transition admission expires; the safe reading is that the transfer-out/release must occur while she is still in authorized status (by July 14, 2027), and she would then need the I-539 for the new program regardless.

Q3.answer: (a) Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), an F-1 may be admitted up to 30 days before the report/program start date. January 12, 2027 minus 30 days = December 13, 2026 (Dec 14–31 = 18 days; Jan 1–12 = 12). So the earliest possible admission date is December 13, 2026; his December 20, 2026 entry is within the window. (b) His admission runs to the program end date plus the 30-day departure period: December 18, 2027 + 30 days (Dec 19–31 = 13; Jan 1–17 = 17) = January 17, 2028. That is the date his I-94 should show. (c) Yes. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(i) accepts a 'compelling academic reason,' defined to include 'unexpected research problems... caused by an unexpected change in faculty advisor.' Reasons the rule says would NOT work: delays caused by academic probation or suspension, or a student's repeated inability or unwillingness to complete the course of study (same paragraph; also Summary of Changes, 91 FR 44979). (d) The DSO issued the new I-20 in October 2027, before the December 18, 2027 end date passed, so this is a timely program extension, not a 'late request.' If the DSO had entered the new end date in SEVIS after the I-20 end date had passed, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii) applies: the student must file a request for reinstatement of F-1 status with USCIS (form, required fee, biometrics), and F-2 dependents must file extensions or reinstatement applications. (e) Timely filing: USCIS must receive the extension application on or before expiration of his authorized stay, including the 30-day period — i.e., by January 17, 2028 (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)). A filing received during the December 18, 2027–January 17, 2028 window is still timely, but he 'does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment' and must wait for approval before continuing or beginning CPT/on-campus employment ((f)(5)(viii), last sentences; (f)(7)(iii)(B)). After January 17, 2028 the application is not timely; he would be out of status and would need reinstatement. (f) If USCIS receives the application by January 17, 2028, his on-campus (RA) employment is automatically extended while the application is pending, but for no more than 240 days beginning from his I-94 end date (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii); subject to (f)(9), (f)(10)(i) and 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(i), (iii), (c)(3)(iii)). Arithmetic: January 17, 2028 + 240 days (Jan 18–31 = 14; Feb 2028 = 29; Mar = 31; Apr = 30; May = 31; Jun = 30; Jul = 31; Aug = 31; subtotal 227; +13 = Sept 13) = September 13, 2028. (g) If approved, he is given an extension for the period necessary to complete the program as listed on his endorsed I-20 (May 19, 2028), not to exceed 4 years (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)), plus the 30-day departure period: May 19, 2028 + 30 days = June 18, 2028. If it is denied after his I-94 date has passed, he and his dependents must depart the United States immediately (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vii)).
Q3.basis: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(v), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(i), (f)(7)(iii), (f)(7)(vi)–(viii), as added by 2026-14439, 91 FR 45125–45127; Summary of Changes, 91 FR 44979; date arithmetic shown above.
Q3.uncertainty: (b)/(f) The rule does not state explicitly whether the I-94 'admit until' for an initial F-1 admission includes the 30-day departure period; 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) ('plus additional 30 day periods for arrival and departure') and (f)(5)(i) ('may remain... for an additional 30 days'; the 30-day period 'will be reflected on' the I-94, (f)(5)(v)) support including it, which is the reading used here.

Q4.answer: (a) Yes, the trip is compatible with the pending I-539 if handled correctly. Under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i), added by the final rule, USCIS will not consider a timely filed extension application abandoned if the student departs while it is pending, provided that (1) when he seeks readmission the previously authorized period of admission has not expired (his runs to January 17, 2028, so a January 5, 2028 return is fine), and (2) he seeks admission 'for the balance of the previously authorized admission period.' How he presents himself matters a great deal: his October 2027 I-20 shows a program end date of May 19, 2028 — beyond his current admission. If at the POE he presents that I-20 and seeks admission for the longer program period, 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii) says the extension application 'may be deemed abandoned' (CBP's new fixed admission supersedes the pending EOS; see preamble, 91 FR 45099–45100). He should seek readmission for the balance of his current admission. The rule says he should carry a copy of the Form I-797C receipt notice confirming receipt of his I-539, along with the proposed length of stay as evidenced by his Form I-20 (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii)); the preamble adds that he must still monitor for and respond to any RFE while abroad (91 FR 45100). (b) For a change of status: 8 CFR 248.1(f), added by 2026-14439, provides that if an alien timely files an application to change to another nonimmigrant status but departs the United States while it is pending, 'USCIS will consider the change of status application abandoned.' There is no balance-of-period exception for change-of-status applicants, unlike extension applicants under 214.1(c)(8)(i).
Q4.basis: 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i)–(iii) (91 FR 45123); 8 CFR 248.1(f) (91 FR 45131); preamble discussion of departure while applications pending, 91 FR 45099–45100 (2026-14439).
Q4.uncertainty: (a) The text does not spell out how a DSO-endorsed I-20 with a later end date should be presented at the POE where an EOS is pending; the safest reading (and the one the preamble's abandonment rationale supports) is to seek the balance of the current admission and treat the later end date as the subject of the pending I-539.

Q5.answer: Yes — she can transfer, but only after she completes the master's, and she must also file an I-539 extension of stay. Provisions in the final regulatory text (all added by 2026-14439) and how each applies: (1) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) — an F-1 at the graduate level or above 'may not transfer at any point during their program of study, unless an exception is authorized by SEVP for extenuating circumstances.' While Mei is enrolled in the master's (August 2025–May 14, 2027), this bars a transfer; she has no extenuating circumstance. (2) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C) — a transfer applicant must not be 'currently in a graduate level program of study, unless an exception has been authorized by SEVP under (f)(5)(ii)(A).' Once she completes the master's on May 14, 2027 she is no longer currently in a graduate program, so this bar no longer applies. (3) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(B)(2) — a student is eligible to transfer if she '[h]as completed a degree program'; Mei qualifies after May 14, 2027. (4) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B) — a student who completes a program at one educational level and begins a new program at a higher level is maintaining F-1 status; master's→PhD is upward, so the PhD is permissible in level terms. (5) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) — bars new programs at the same or lower level for programs completed after September 15, 2026; not triggered (PhD is higher). (6) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G) — she must begin classes at School B within 5 months of transferring out or of the May 14, 2027 program completion date, whichever is earlier: deadline October 14, 2027; her August 23, 2027 start is within it. (7) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(ii) and (iii) — transfer procedure; a change of education level is accomplished through those procedures (transfer-out/release date mechanics). (8) 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv), (f)(7) — because she is in the D/S transition group and the PhD start date (August 23, 2027) falls after her authorized stay ends (May 14, 2027 + 60 days = July 13, 2027), she must file an I-539 extension of stay with USCIS for the PhD admission period; (f)(7)(iii)(B) requires receipt on or before expiration of her authorized stay. Conclusion: her SEVIS record can be transferred to School B once the master's is completed (transfer-out/release under (f)(8)(ii)), with classes beginning by October 14, 2027; while enrolled in the master's a transfer is barred by (f)(5)(ii)(A)/(f)(8)(i)(C) absent a SEVP exception; and the PhD stay itself requires an I-539. Changes: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) lets DHS delay or suspend (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) until September 14, 2028 by Federal Register notification and a SEVP website announcement (with at least 30 days' notice of implementation) — no such notification appears in the Federal Register through November 14, 2026. Separately, the pending OPT-fee NPRM (2026-20660, 91 FR 64576–64577) floats an alternative under which the $70,000 initial OPT fee would reapply at each higher educational level — it would not change transfer eligibility but could add cost to her move to the PhD if finalized; it is only a proposal.
Q5.uncertainty: 'Currently in a graduate level program' is not defined; the answer turns on reading it to exclude a student who has completed the program (supported by (f)(8)(i)(B)(2) expressly making program completion a transfer qualification). DHS has not yet said whether it will exercise the (f)(5)(ii)(E) delay authority.

Q6.answer: (a) No, under either route. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C), added by the final rule, provides that 'an alien who has completed a program after September 15, 2026... at one educational level may not maintain, be admitted, or otherwise be provided F-1 status through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level.' Ahmed completes a master's on December 11, 2026 and wants another master's-level program (MBA): that is the same educational level, so he can neither transfer ((f)(8)(i), which incorporates (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C)) nor be readmitted at a POE into F-1 for the MBA (214.1(a)(4)). (b) The transfer timing rule, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G), requires that he begin classes at the transfer school within 5 months of transferring out or of the program completion date on his current I-20 (December 11, 2026), whichever is earlier — i.e., by May 11, 2027. An August 2027 start fails that timing requirement on its own terms, independent of the level bar in (a). (c) Under the transition rule, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1), he remains authorized until his program end date (December 11, 2026) plus the 60-day F departure period: Dec 12–31 = 20 days, Jan = 31, Feb 1–9 = 9 → February 9, 2027. (d) Yes, possibly. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) authorizes DHS to delay or suspend (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) — including the same-level prohibition — until September 14, 2028, by publishing a notification in the Federal Register and announcing it on SEVP's website, with at least 30 days' advance notice of any implementation date. DHS could act before August 2027 and restore his ability to pursue the MBA; as of November 14, 2026 no such notification has been published. The other pending rulemakings (2026-18631; 2026-20660) do not address same-level study.
Q6.basis: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)–(E), (f)(8)(i)(G); 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4), (m)(1) — 91 FR 45124–45125, 45122 (2026-14439); Summary of Changes, 91 FR 44979; searches of the Federal Register July 18–November 14, 2026 for any delay/suspension notification (none found).
Q6.uncertainty: The rule does not say whether DHS will exercise its (f)(5)(ii)(E) discretion or when; timing of any such action is unknowable from the documents.

Q7.answer: (a) The document currently imposing the payment requirement is Proclamation 11069, 'Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers,' signed September 18, 2026, published September 23, 2026 as document 2026-19554, 91 FR 60497–60500. It restricts entry of H-1B specialty-occupation workers except where the petition is 'accompanied or supplemented by a payment of $100,000' (Sec. 1(a)); effective 12:01 a.m. EDT September 21, 2026; expires absent extension 12 months after that effective date, i.e., September 21, 2027. Other presidential documents bearing on it: Proclamation 10973 (document 2025-18601, 90 FR 46027, signed September 19, 2025, effective September 21, 2025, which imposed the original payment and expired September 21, 2026 absent extension), and Executive Order 14431, 'Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Program' (document 2026-19555, 91 FR 60501, signed September 18, 2026), which directs interagency scrutiny of H-1B petitions and employer layoffs but does not itself impose a payment. (b) On the text, no. The restriction applies to 'entry' of aliens as H-1B workers (Sec. 1(a)), 'only to aliens who enter or attempt to enter the United States after the effective date' (Sec. 3(a)); the decision-restriction and documentation provisions in Secs. 1(b) and 2(a)–(b) are aimed at petitions on behalf of aliens 'currently outside the United States.' Lena is in the U.S. in F-1 status with a change-of-status request, so her petition does not trigger the payment requirement. It could reach her if she travels abroad and must seek admission (e.g., consular processing) to effectuate the H-1B — Sec. 3(a) of the 2026 Proclamation expressly covers aliens who must seek admission to effectuate a covered petition — unless her employer pays the $100,000 or DHS grants a national-interest exception under Sec. 1(c). (c) Yes: document 2026-17324, 'Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions' (NPRM, published August 25, 2026, 91 FR 54817–54839; Docket CIS No. 2861-26 / USCIS-2026-0298; RIN 1615-AD20) proposes a $103,265 fee, payable at the time of filing, at proposed 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii), for all H-1B cap-subject petitions (including those eligible for the advanced degree exemption), in addition to all other fees. It would NOT apply to Lena's cap-exempt petition: the proposal expressly covers only cap-subject petitions and 'not to all H-1B petitions such as cap-exempt filings' (91 FR 54819), and states the fee does not apply to petitions exempt under INA 214(g)(5) and (7) (91 FR 54831–54832). Status: proposed rule only — not in force; written comments were due September 24, 2026; it was corrected by C1-2026-17324 (91 FR 57516, Sept. 10, 2026), which corrected only Table 13 receipt-volume data. (Also note 2026-20660 proposes new fees for OPT, not H-1B petitions.) (d) The F-1 cap-gap provision, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vii) (redesignated and retained by 2026-14439, 91 FR 45125–45126), automatically extends an F-1's status (and any 274a.12(c)(3)(i) employment authorization) until April 1 of the fiscal year requested or the petition's validity start date, whichever is earlier — but only where the student is the beneficiary of an H-1B petition 'subject to section 214(g)(1)(A)' (cap-subject), timely filed, with a start date consistent with (h)(2)(i)(I), and nonfrivolous. A petition filed by a cap-exempt employer is not subject to 214(g)(1)(A), so on the text Lena gets no automatic extension; she must maintain F-1 status by her own filings (e.g., an I-539 extension under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), (f)(7)) through July 1, 2027. (e) Under 8 CFR 248.1(f), added by 2026-14439, if she departs the United States while the change-of-status request is pending, USCIS will consider the application abandoned.
Q7.uncertainty: The proclamations do not define 'change of status' versus 'entry' for an F-1 beneficiary whose approved petition would later be activated by travel; the reading above follows the text of Secs. 1(b), 2(a) and 3(a). Whether the $103,265 fee proposal or an OPT-fee final rule will be finalized, and on what terms, is unknown.

Q8.answer: (a) The document is document 2026-18631, 'Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period' (NPRM, published September 11, 2026, 91 FR 57807–57828). It proposes to remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) — the regulation giving aliens in certain employment-based nonimmigrant classifications (E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B and similar categories) and their dependents an up-to-60-day grace period when their qualifying employment ceases before their authorized stay expires — restoring the pre-2017 policy that such aliens fall out of status when the employment ends. (b) Status: proposed rule only; not final and not in force as of November 14, 2026. Written comments were due November 10, 2026 (DATES, 91 FR 57807). (c) It does not affect Priya's 60 days. Her 60-day departure period comes from the D/S transition rule, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (added by 2026-14439), which preserves the departure period 'as provided in their previous admission' (see 91 FR 45101); 214.1(l)(2) is a different provision about cessation of employment, and the NPRM's own text treats the F-1 program-completion grace (formerly (f)(5)(iv)) as a separate arrangement it is not changing (91 FR 57814). (d) It bears on students only after they leave F-1 for employment-based status: e.g., Lena (Q7), once in H-1B, or any student who later moves to H/L/E/O/TN status, would lose the 60-day post-employment grace period if the rule is finalized. It does not touch the F-1 departure periods of Priya, Sofia, Daniel, Ahmed, Mei, Tomás or Lin.
Q8.basis: 2026-18631 (91 FR 57807), abstract and DATES; preamble discussion contrasting F-1/J-1 grace periods at 91 FR 57811 and 57814; 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (2026-14439, 91 FR 45123).
Q8.uncertainty: Whether DHS will finalize the rule, and whether a final version would differ (e.g., in covered classifications), cannot be determined from the Federal Register as of November 14, 2026.

Q9.answer: Changes described in the final rule's comparison section (section V.A, 'Summary of Changes in the Final Rule as Compared to the NPRM,' 91 FR 45096–45098, document 2026-14439): (1) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) — the prohibition on same-or-lower-level programs now applies only to students who complete a program after the rule's effective date (September 15, 2026), rather than retroactively (91 FR 45097). (2) New 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) — DHS's power to delay or suspend the transfer/educational-objective restrictions was limited to two years (until September 14, 2028) and a Federal Register announcement was added to the SEVP-website announcement (91 FR 45097; text at 91 FR 45125). (3) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v) — clarified that a student who finishes study or training early must depart (with dependents) within 30 days of the early end date, and that a student who fails to maintain status gets no departure period at all and must leave immediately (91 FR 45097; text at 91 FR 45125). (4) 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)–(iii) — the transitional I-539 exemption was restructured into a standalone paragraph reserving DHS discretion to extend the I-539 filing exemption beyond the stated dates in 6-month increments by Federal Register notification (91 FR 45097; text at 91 FR 45123–45124). (5) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) — revised so an F-1 recommended for post-completion OPT may either apply for an extension of stay with USCIS or seek admission through CBP after travel abroad (91 FR 45097; text at 91 FR 45126). (6) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D) — changed '60' to '30,' so a reinstatement start date may be no more than 30 days after the program end date (91 FR 45096–45097). (7) 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) — the proposed paragraph was dropped because existing 214.1(c)(7) already covers USCIS discretion over extension decisions (91 FR 45096). (8) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) — added 'a student needing to change schools to complete elementary or secondary education' to the extenuating-circumstances examples and sharpened the graduate-level transfer/objective prohibitions (91 FR 45097; text at 91 FR 45124–45125). (9) 8 CFR 248.1(e) — dropped proposed language about forms accompanying change-of-status approvals (91 FR 45097–45098; text at 91 FR 45130–45131). (10) 8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(vii)(A) — clarified J-1 employment during a pending EOS runs only up to 240 days, and preserved the special first-six-months provision for EOS filed by March 18, 2027 (91 FR 45097; text at 91 FR 45129–45130).
Q9.basis: 2026-14439, section V.A, 91 FR 45096–45098; corresponding final regulatory text at 91 FR 45122–45131.
Q9.uncertainty: The preamble also lists purely 'technical edits' (e.g., title consistency, wording of (f)(8)(i)(D) and (H)) not itemized above; the five-plus changes listed are the substantive/clarifying ones.

Q10.answer: Documents published July 18, 2026–November 14, 2026 relevant to an F-1 planning post-graduation work: (1) 2026-19554, Proclamation 11069 (published Sept. 23, 2026; signed Sept. 18, 2026; 91 FR 60497) — extends through September 21, 2027 the entry restriction requiring a $100,000 payment for H-1B petitions of workers seeking admission, which matters to any F-1 who will need consular processing for an H-1B. In force. (2) 2026-19555, Executive Order 14431 (published Sept. 23, 2026; 91 FR 60501) — directs State/Labor/DHS to coordinate and scrutinize H-1B petitions, LCAs and visas, including employer layoffs, increasing scrutiny for students seeking H-1B changes of status. In force. (3) 2026-17324, 'Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions' (NPRM, published Aug. 25, 2026; 91 FR 54817; corrected by C1-2026-17324, 91 FR 57516, Sept. 10, 2026) — proposes a $103,265 filing-time fee for cap-subject H-1B petitions (cap-exempt petitions excluded). Not in force; comments closed Sept. 24, 2026. (4) 2026-20660, 'Optional Practical Training Fees' (NPRM, published Oct. 8, 2026; 91 FR 64566) — proposes that schools pay $70,000 for a first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT (including STEM OPT) before the DSO enters the recommendation in SEVIS, with USCIS barred from granting EADs where the fee is unpaid. Not in force; comments closed Nov. 9, 2026. (5) 2026-20955, 'Removal of Automatic Extensions for Certain Employment Authorization Documents' (final rule, published and effective Oct. 14, 2026; 91 FR 65306) — finalizes the Oct. 30, 2025 IFR (90 FR 48799) ending automatic extension of EAD validity upon timely filed renewal applications in the covered 274a.12 categories; it contains no F-1-specific amendment, but students holding any EAD category that relied on automatic renewal extensions lose that cushion. In force. (6) 2026-18631, 'Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period' (NPRM, published Sept. 11, 2026; 91 FR 57807) — proposes removing the 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) post-employment grace period for E/H/L/O-type workers, relevant to students after they move into those statuses. Not in force; comments closed Nov. 10, 2026.
Q10.basis: fr_search results and fr_doc metadata for each document; 2026-20955 regulatory text at 91 FR 65368 ('adopts the amendments... as published on October 30, 2025, at 90 FR 48799 as final'); 2026-20660, 91 FR 64576–64577; 2026-19554, 91 FR 60497–60500; 2026-17324, 91 FR 54817–54839 and C1-2026-17324, 91 FR 57516; 2026-18631, 91 FR 57807.
Q10.uncertainty: (5) The final rule does not list which 274a.12 categories were amended within the excerpts read; its effect on any particular EAD category (other than that it ends renewal-based automatic extensions) cannot be confirmed without reading the October 30, 2025 IFR, which is outside the July 18–November 14, 2026 window.

Q11.answer: What the final rule actually says: (1) Cost. The final regulatory text never fixes a dollar amount; it requires the applicant to file 'the form and in the manner designated by USCIS... and remitting the appropriate fee,' plus evidence of funds and any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16 (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2); 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), 91 FR 45123, 45126). The preamble explains that the Form I-539 filing fee 'is intended to cover the cost of processing and adjudicating EOS' requests under USCIS's fee-for-service, full-cost-recovery fee schedule, which USCIS studies biennially (91 FR 45015, 45083–45084); it also states dependents may be included on the principal's application for no additional fee if statuses expire simultaneously (91 FR 45029–45030). Dollar figures that do appear are in comments, not regulatory text: a commenter put the I-539 filing fee at $420 (91 FR 45055), and another estimated an affected au-pair program's cost rising 'from $367 to over $800' with filing fees and biometrics (91 FR 45056). The Regulatory Impact Analysis gives aggregate, not per-case, figures: annualized costs of $443.1–$448.6 million (3% and 7% discount rates) (91 FR 44980). (2) Processing time. The rule sets no decision deadline and no service-level target: 'DHS cannot guarantee processing times for applications filed at USCIS due to numerous governing factors' (91 FR 45025), while acknowledging the rule 'may cause an increase in USCIS processing times' (91 FR 45010, 45021) and encouraging nonimmigrants to 'apply well in advance of the expiration of their stay' — the rule's discussion uses about 180 days before expiration as 'as early as possible' (91 FR 45021, 45043). A commenter's statement put current I-539 processing around 3.5 months (91 FR 44992). Draft handout sentences: 'To stay past the date on your I-94, you must file an extension of stay (Form I-539) with USCIS, with the filing fee set in USCIS's fee schedule, a DSO-endorsed I-20, proof of funding, and any required biometrics (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), 214.2(f)(7)); USCIS must receive it by the date your authorized stay ends. The rule sets no fixed fee or decision deadline and does not guarantee processing times, so file as early as possible — the government's own discussion points to about 180 days before your stay expires.'
Q11.uncertainty: The rule gives no per-application fee amount or adjudication timeline; the $420 and 3.5-month figures are commenter statements, not DHS positions, and actual fees/times depend on USCIS's current fee schedule, which is outside the Federal Register documents read.

Q12.answer: (a) Yes — on the most defensible reading. Priya is a transition student under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1): her authorized stay runs until the later of EAD expiration or her I-20 program end date (May 15, 2027), plus the 60-day departure period (to July 14, 2027). 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) makes an extension application timely if USCIS's receipt date 'is on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires.' Because her authorized period of stay includes the 60-day transition window, an I-539 received within those 60 days (through July 14, 2027) is timely. The preamble confirms the transition preserves the previous admission's 60 days 'as provided in their previous admission' (91 FR 45100–45102). Caveat: (f)(7)(iii)(B) literally references 'the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v),' and the rule never says expressly that the transition 60-day window is an EOS filing window; the reading above follows from (m)(1) defining her authorized stay. (b) Probably yes, but the text is not explicit. The automatic-employment bar in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) applies only where the student files 'during the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)' — a window that does not exist for transition students, whose departure period is the 60-day (m)(1) period. Filing during that 60-day window is not filing during a (f)(5)(v) 30-day period, so on the text the bar should not apply and her on-campus/CPT employment authorization would be automatically extended while the I-539 is pending, up to 240 days from her I-94 end date (f)(5)(viii), subject to (f)(9), (f)(10)(i) and 274a.12(b)(6)(i), (iii), (c)(3)(iii). Because the rule is silent on this precise combination, this is not free from doubt. Recommendation to the adviser: have Priya file the I-539 (and her I-765) before the May 15, 2027 program end date. Filing before the program end avoids the timely-filing question entirely, keeps the 240-day employment safety net clean, and avoids any argument that a transition-window filing is treated like a (f)(5)(v)-window filing (where employment stops until approval). If a filing in the last 60 days becomes unavoidable, it is timely under (m)(1)/(f)(7)(iii)(B), but advise her not to rely on continuing to work pending adjudication without checking current USCIS guidance.
Q12.basis: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (91 FR 45123); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(5)(viii) (91 FR 45126); preamble at 91 FR 45100–45102 (departure periods 'as provided in their previous admission'); pending EAD transition provisions 214.1(m)(2) (91 FR 45124).
Q12.uncertainty: The rule does not expressly address (i) EOS filings made during the transition 60-day window other than the OPT-specific (m)(1)(i) exemption, or (ii) whether the (f)(5)(viii) employment bar reaches transition-window filings; both answers above are the most defensible textual readings, flagged as such.

Q13.answer: (a) Sofia departed and was readmitted after September 15, 2026, so under the final rule she receives a new fixed admission period like any newly admitted F-1 (preamble, 91 FR 45099–45100: D/S students who depart after the effective date are admitted 'with a new fixed admission period... based on the date on their Form I-20... and 30 days for departure'; 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (v)). She is admitted until the program end date (May 14, 2027) plus 30 days: May 15–31 = 17 days, June 1–13 = 13 → June 13, 2027. That supersedes the transition 60-day arrangement. (b) Yes. Because she departed before filing for OPT and was readmitted with a fixed period of admission, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii) applies: she 'is required to file both an Application for Employment Authorization, Form I-765... and an Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status, Form I-539... pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) or (f)(11)(i)(C).' The extension application must be received by USCIS on or before the expiration of her authorized period of stay — June 13, 2027 (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)); filing it together with the February 22, 2027 I-765 satisfies this comfortably. (c) If the OPT is approved as requested (EAD June 10, 2027–June 9, 2028), she may remain until the EAD expiration plus 60 days (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i); (f)(10)(ii)(D) includes the 30-day departure period after OPT for EOS/admission routes): June 9, 2028 + 60 days (June 10–30 = 21; July = 31; Aug 1–8 = 8) = August 8, 2028. (d) Alternative facts: no I-539 is needed. She filed the I-765 on February 22, 2027, before March 18, 2027, so 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) excuses her from filing an I-539 'for the requested period of post-completion OPT'; she had not departed before filing, so (m)(1)(ii) never attached. Traveling May 20–June 5, 2027 while the I-765 is pending: under (m)(1)(ii) (last sentence) and 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii), on return she will be admitted — if the I-765 is still pending, until the DSO's recommended employment end date on the I-20 (June 9, 2028); if it has been approved, until the EAD end date (June 9, 2028) — in either case plus the 30-day period under (f)(5)(v): June 9, 2028 + 30 days = July 9, 2028. Between EAD expiry and the I-94 date she is in a period of authorized stay (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(D)). She should carry a copy of the Form I-797C receipt notice confirming USCIS received the I-765, and her I-20 endorsed by the DSO with the recommended OPT end date (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii); preamble, 91 FR 45099), and if the EAD has been approved she must have it in hand to re-enter (preamble n.303, 91 FR 45100).
Q13.uncertainty: (b) 214.1(m)(1)(ii) cross-references '(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) or (f)(11)(i)(C)' (the reinstatement/extension provisions as renumbered); the receipt deadline used here comes from (f)(7)(iii)(B), which governs extension filings generally. (d) The exact admission date CBP grants depends on whether the EAD is approved before re-entry; both outcomes end at the same date (June 9, 2028) plus 30 days.

Q14.answer: (a) The document is 2026-20660, 'Optional Practical Training Fees' (NPRM, published October 8, 2026, 91 FR 64566–64600; agency: DHS/ICE; docket DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01). Status: proposed rule — not final, not in force as of November 14, 2026. Deadlines it sets: written comments due November 9, 2026; Paperwork Reduction Act information-collection comments due December 7, 2026; and the proposal itself provides that a final rule would take effect 60 days after publication (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)). (b) $30,000. The NPRM sets $70,000 for the first OPT recommendation of any type and $30,000 'for any subsequent OPT recommendation for an F-1 nonimmigrant student who has previously participated in OPT and has previously paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000' (91 FR 64576–64577, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)). Daniel already holds a post-completion OPT EAD, so his April 2027 STEM OPT recommendation is a subsequent recommendation → the $30,000 fee, and it is the school that pays. (c) The SEVP-certified school pays, and must pay before the DSO enters the OPT recommendation in SEVIS; the DSO may not enter the recommendation, or confirm it for the I-20, until the fee is paid, and USCIS 'would not grant employment authorization to any student' where the fee was not paid before the recommendation or at all (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii), 214.13(i); 91 FR 64577). Refunds: the school may request a refund only if the student has not received the OPT/STEM OPT EAD (the DSO must first remove the recommendation in SEVIS); once the student has received the OPT EAD the fee 'would not be refunded under any circumstances'; SEVP adjudicates refund requests case-by-case, in its discretion, and its determination is final and not appealable (91 FR 64577). (d) The fee would apply to students whose DSO recommendation for OPT 'is dated on or after the effective date of the final rule' (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3); 91 FR 64577) — the effective date being 60 days after publication of a final rule. So Daniel stays outside the fee only if his DSO's recommendation is dated before that effective date; once a final rule is in effect, no timing of the recommendation avoids it (a later recommendation only delays, and the DSO could not enter it without payment). (e) Under the rules in force today: his DSO recommends the 24-month STEM OPT extension on his Form I-20, and he files Form I-765 with the required fee for the extension. Because he would file on April 12, 2027 — after March 18, 2027 — the transitional I-539 exemption in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) no longer covers him, so under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) he must also apply for an extension of stay (Form I-539) with USCIS (contents per (f)(7)(iii)(A); receipt deadline per (f)(7)(iii)(B) — by expiration of his authorized stay; his transition admission runs to his EAD expiry, June 30, 2027). While the I-765 is pending he keeps working under the 180-day automatic extension of his post-completion OPT EAD — until USCIS's written decision or 180 days, whichever is earlier (8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv); see 2026-14439, 91 FR 45037). If approved, he may remain until the expiration of the new STEM OPT EAD plus 60 days (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)).
Q14.uncertainty: The proposal is not final; its amounts, payment mechanics and effective date could all change. Whether the October 2026 final rule on EAD automatic extensions (2026-20955) affects the STEM OPT 180-day provision cannot be confirmed from the excerpts read — that rule amends 274a.12 renewal-extension categories and contains no F-1-specific amendment.

Q15.answer: 1. INCORRECT. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) makes the application timely if USCIS receives it 'on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, which includes the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)' — i.e., through the I-94 date, not the I-20 program end date. Reword: 'USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application by the date the student's authorized stay (the I-94 date) expires; a student may keep studying if it is received in the final 30-day window, but employment stops until approval.' 2. INCORRECT. The 4-year maximum is not counted from the entry date: the regulatory text admits the student for 'the period necessary to complete the course of study... not to exceed a period of 4 years' (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)), and the preamble states the 4-year maximum 'will not begin from the date of admission during that 30-day arrival window, but from the program start date' (91 FR 45098–45099; also 91 FR 45015–45016). Reword: 'The four-year maximum runs from the program start date, not from the day of entry, and the 30-day arrival and departure windows do not count toward it.' 3. CORRECT. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) keeps the student in a period of authorized stay until USCIS decides (no time cap on staying/studying), but the automatic extension of on-campus, CPT and severe-economic-hardship employment 'may not exceed 240 days beginning from the end date of his or her period of admission as indicated on... Form I-94.' After 240 days the employment must stop; study may continue while the application is pending. No preamble conflict. 4. INCORRECT. The preamble forecloses medical extensions of the ELT cap: 'Students who encounter extenuating circumstances such as illness, disability, or other emergencies during their studies, will still be limited to the 24-month admission period' (91 FR 45039; cap at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)). Reword: 'An English-language-training student is capped at an aggregate 24-month admission even for illness or other emergencies; a documented illness is a ground for extension for degree-program students (214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii)), not a way past the 24-month ELT cap.' (Note the tension: (f)(7)(vi) caps extensions at 4 years, but the preamble's ELT response controls the ELT cap; the regulatory cap is at (f)(5)(i)(A).) 5. INCORRECT. Nothing in the rule shortens longer programs or requires two I-20s. The student is admitted only up to the 4-year maximum (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)), and the preamble says students in programs longer than 4 years must 'apply to extend their stay or depart the United States and seek readmission' at the 4-year point (91 FR 45098–45099); a pathway-plus-degree program is admitted as one combined period up to 4 years, with EOS available beyond (91 FR 45039–45040). Reword: 'A program longer than four years is issued on one I-20, but the student is admitted for at most four years and must file an extension of stay with USCIS (or depart and re-enter) to finish.' 6. CORRECT (with a caveat). The preamble states that a departing student 'may be admitted for the length of time as indicated by the program end date noted in their Form I-20... not to exceed 4 years, plus a period of 30 days' (91 FR 45098–45099; 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A); 214.2(f)(5)(i)) — a new admission from CBP, not a USCIS extension. Caveat from the same preamble and 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii): if an extension of stay is pending and the student instead seeks admission for the longer program period, the pending EOS may be deemed abandoned. Reword: 'Travel and readmission on a later-end-date I-20 gets a fresh CBP admission (program end date, capped at 4 years, plus 30 days) — so no USCIS extension is needed for that time — but if an extension application is pending, readmission on the longer I-20 can abandon it.' 7. INCORRECT. The fixed date in the regulatory text is March 18, 2027, not six months after the effective date (which would be March 15, 2027): 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) excuses the I-539 for OPT/STEM OPT I-765s filed 'on or before March 18, 2027,' and 214.1(m)(1)(iii) reserves DHS discretion to extend the exemption 'beyond March 18, 2027, in 6-month increments by publication of a notification in the Federal Register' — no such notification has been published through November 14, 2026. Reword: 'OPT applicants who file Form I-765 on or before March 18, 2027 do not need to file an I-539; DHS may extend that date in six-month steps by Federal Register notice.'
Q15.uncertainty: For statement 4, the regulatory text alone ((f)(7)(vi) 4-year extension limit vs (f)(5)(i)(A) 24-month ELT cap) is in tension; the preamble's express statement that illness does not lift the ELT cap is the clearest indication of DHS's intent and was treated as controlling.

Q16.answer: (a) Her program (to May 14, 2033) exceeds 4 years, so she is admitted for the 4-year maximum, which the preamble says is 'calculated from the date the program begins... program start date' and does not include the 30-day arrival window or the 30-day departure period (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i); 91 FR 45015–45016, 45098–45099). Arithmetic: program start August 23, 2027 + 4 years = August 23, 2031; plus the 30-day departure period (Aug 24–31 = 8; Sept 1–22 = 22) = September 22, 2031. Her I-94 should show September 22, 2031. (b) She must apply to USCIS for an extension of stay on Form I-539 (or successor) with the required fee, a DSO-endorsed new I-20 showing the additional time, evidence of sufficient funds, and any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16 (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2); 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)); her F-2 husband must be included on her application or file his own ((f)(7)(iv); 214.1(c)(2) family-unit filing). Ground: (f)(7)(i) — she maintained status, is pursuing a full course of study, and is unable to complete the program by the end of her authorized admission, evidenced by a currently issued I-20. Earliest filing: the regulatory text sets only the latest date (receipt on or before expiration of the authorized stay, including the 30-day period, (f)(7)(iii)(B)); the preamble indicates students should 'apply as early as possible (180 days) before the expiration of their current stay' (91 FR 45043), so filing up to about 180 days ahead is contemplated, with no stated minimum. If granted in full, she is given the period necessary to complete the program as listed on the I-20, not to exceed 4 years ((f)(7)(vi)) — through May 14, 2033, plus the 30-day departure period: May 14, 2033 + 30 days = June 13, 2033. (c) No adverse effect. The same-or-lower-level bar in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) reaches a student who completes a program and then 'maintain[s], [is] admitted, or otherwise... provided F-1 status through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level' — i.e., a separate, new program. Lin's master's is awarded en route within one continuous PhD program; her I-20, program end date, and course of study do not change, and (f)(5)(ii)(B) in any event treats upward progression as status-maintaining. Nothing in the rule requires her to count the master's as a completed program that resets or limits the PhD. (d) Under the rule's stated method, the 4-year maximum continues to run from her original program start date (August 23, 2027), so on readmission in August 2030 she is admitted only through the remaining fixed admission — to August 23, 2031, with the I-94 showing September 22, 2031 (214.1(a)(4); (f)(5)(i); preamble 91 FR 45098–45099, 45015–45016). She therefore still needs the (b) filing to reach May 14, 2033; the 4-year cap plus periodic DHS review is the rule's core design and the transition rule's fixed 4-year-from-effective-date cap reflects the same anti-reset philosophy. Certainty: moderately high on the outcome (the filing is still needed), but flagged: the text does not expressly address mid-program readmissions, and a contrary reading (a fresh 4 years from readmission, capped by the program end date — which would run to May 14, 2033 and eliminate the need to file) cannot be excluded from the text alone. (e) His later I-94 does not extend him: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E) — 'The authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents may not exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student,' and the preamble states that if the principal's stay ends, dependents 'must depart at the same time as the principal even if their I-94 has a longer period of stay' (91 FR 45016). So he may stay only until Lin's authorized stay ends (September 22, 2031 on the facts in (a)), notwithstanding the later date on his I-94. When Lin applies under (b), he is covered by being included on her Form I-539 as a family member: 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) allows single-family co-applicants with extensions granted for the same period (the shortest period is granted to all); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv) requires F-2s to be included or to file their own applications. Fee: dependents included on the principal's application are covered 'for one fee' — the Form I-539 'allows dependents... to be included for one fee and concurrent adjudication' (91 FR 45015), and dependents may be included 'for no additional fee if statuses expire simultaneously' (91 FR 45029); a separately filed dependent application would bear its own fee.
Q16.basis: 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), (m)(1); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (i)(E), (f)(7)(i), (iii), (iv), (vi), (f)(5)(ii)(B)–(C) — 91 FR 45122–45127 (2026-14439); preamble at 91 FR 45015–45016, 45043, 45098–45099 (4-year count from program start date; dependent rules); 91 FR 45015 and 45029–45030 (one-fee family filing).
Q16.uncertainty: (d) as explained — the rule does not expressly state whether the 4-year clock resets on readmission mid-program; the answer follows the preamble's stated counting method. (b) The regulatory text sets no earliest filing date; the 180-day figure is preamble guidance, not a rule.
